newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav pensioners protest over tardy payments.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav pensioners protest over tardy payments.

text.p: Thousands of disillusioned pensioners demonstrated in the Yugoslav capital Belgrade on Thursday to protest at non-payment of their benefits and demand better living standards.

Displaying empty purses and waving pension slips which showed they had not received any money since February, protesters said they could not take it any more in a cash-starved economy pauperised by inflation and state mismanagement.
"The issue of pensions does not touch anyone. It is sad we have to watch television to hear when our pensions will be paid out," said Visnja Djordjevic, a retired ballet dancer.
"The authorities care just about themselves, regardless if they are the ruling Socialists or opposition."
President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialists are under growing pressure from striking doctors and nurses, teachers and idled, discontented workers throughout Yugoslavia to make cash payouts.

"The authorities have forced pensioners to finally raise their voice. They are neglecting us but forgetting that we have one lethal weapon -- our vote," said Dragan Nikitovic, a retired sports reporter.
Regular payments to some 1.6 million pensioners pose a major burden for Yugoslavia's budget in a widely moribund economy.
Some analysts say pensions this year would account for 20 percent of Yugoslavia's gross domestic product, estimated at a greatly reduced 103 billion dinars ($20.6 billion).

Oversized public spending forced the government to make changes in statistics methodology in January to reduce payments to the elderly. But the government has nonetheless only managed to pay pensions for the first two months.
"Money from the pension fund is used for emergency financing. It is a pay-as-you-go scheme," one analyst said.
Zoran Popov, an Economics Institute expert, said pensions were set too high compared to wages and number of employed.

"It is very difficult to pay pensions regularly when one employed finances one pensioner and one unemployed. It is too big a burden for a poor economy like ours," he said. "Sometimes pensions are by 10 percent higher than wages."
Analysts agree there is virtually no money left in state coffers and said the economy simply cannot sustain the pension burden.
Slobodan Milosavljevic of the Market Research Institute said he did not believe any improvements could be expected this year.
"Re-allocation of budget and social security fund revenues does not give any hope the pensioners will receive more than nine monthly pensions for the whole year," he said.
"There are simply no real sources to finance them."
Popov was even more pessimistic and said the state could finance only 60 percent of its obligations to pensioners, which means a maximum of seven to eight monthly pensions this year.

"The only solution would be to cut the oversized social security benefits inherited from the old (communist) system. And that is a very unpopular and painful measure that no one is ready to resort to. It would be political suicide."
Analysts said the Socialists will have to create additional funds to finance increasing demands for late payouts in a year when presidential and parliamentary elections are due.
Many analysts expect money from the announced sale of Serbia's post and telecommunications agency to be used to patch up the financial void and keep the social peace for the time being.
